title: Who calls the leak
topic: EPA approved an Austin company's autonomous infrared drone for periodic methane screening of oil and gas equipment, and its letter puts a certified inspector, not the software, in the call
credits:
TEXAS AI DOCKET
SOURCES
EPA approval letter, September 30th, 2025
EPA Methane Super Emitter Program page
EPA release, October 7th
DroneLife, March 14th, 2025
ILLUSTRATION
Original authored diagrams, no brand marks

requests.purpose: Give the film one generic inspection drone design that leaves its weatherproof station, flies a flight plan between points of interest with an infrared camera, and stands in the window at the close, so the equipment the EPA letter approves is a recognizable object that changes state through the film.
requests.prompt: Author an original finished React and SVG object in the current Remotion engine. A compact four-rotor inspection drone with a pale gray shell, a slung infrared camera pod with a dark lens, small status lamps, visible rotor discs that blur at speed, short landing legs and a weatherproof charging station with a hinged hood, a pad of worn steel and a leaning post beside it. Late warm desert light from the upper left, cool fill from the right, a soft shadow on the pad. No logos, no brand marks and no real model badge. Maintained but worn, nothing symmetric. A disclosed illustration, never a real drone or station.
requests.source_limit: Disclosed illustration of a generic inspection drone and its station. Not a Percepto or Chevron drone, not the approved Air Max, and not a real site, rotor count or flight height.

requests.purpose: Give the drone its world and its records: a Permian well pad with a separator, valves and a tank, a Texas locator, a flight software panel, an approval letter with a date stamp, an illustrated infrared valve, a review panel with an inspector mark and a follow-up tag, a highlighted protocol title, a leak reporting program tag with calendar pages and a proposal tag, and a blank AI box.
requests.prompt: Author an original finished React and SVG support group in the current Remotion engine. A West Texas well pad with a separator vessel, valves, a tank and a pumpjack silhouette on caliche ground, a flat Texas locator with two pins, a software panel with a status row and an amber alert flag, an unsealed plain approval letter with worn corners and a crooked date stamp, a gray infrared valve view with a warm illustrative shimmer, a review panel with a certified inspector mark and follow-up tag, a protocol title with a highlighted AI, wall calendar pages, a program tag and an unstamped proposal tag, and a dashed blank AI box. Maintained but worn, nothing symmetric, warm paper against cool gray steel. No agency seal, no logos, no brand marks.
requests.source_limit: Disclosed illustration of the sourced records and method. It shows no real site, leak, plume, EPA seal, letter page or person, and the infrared shimmer is not a measured plume.

film_direction.angle: Follow one generic inspection drone from its weatherproof station on a Permian well pad through its flight plan and into the review panel, at ground level, so the viewer sees the machine before the record.
film_direction.opening_promise: Watch a drone leave its station over oil and gas equipment, then see who decides what it found.
film_direction.performed_turn: The certified inspector mark lands on the footage and outlines the emission, and a follow-up tag goes to the valve, so a person makes the call.
film_direction.closing_answer: Under this approval a certified inspector confirms the leak, and the letter doesn't say what the AI adds, shown as an inspector mark beside a blank AI box.

story_contract.opening_question: When a drone flags a leak over oil and gas equipment, who decides it is one?
story_contract.actor: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, which approved an Austin company's drone as an alternative method
story_contract.action: Approved the company's autonomous infrared drone for periodic methane screening, with a certified inspector reviewing the footage.
story_contract.change: Methane screening at oil and gas sites can use a drone that flies a flight plan from a station beside the equipment, with a certified inspector still confirming the leak.
story_contract.affected_people: Operators and the certified inspectors who review drone footage and answer a follow-up inspection. No person is named.
story_contract.consequence: A certified inspector's review of the footage identifies any emissions and triggers a follow-up inspection.
story_contract.source_limit: The EPA letter mentions AI only in a protocol title and doesn't say what the AI adds. No source shows Chevron's drone is the approved Air Max, and no Permian site, leak count or repair is published.
story_contract.closing_answer: Under this approval a certified inspector confirms the leak, and the letter doesn't say what the AI adds.

scenes.advances: The drone lifts from the weatherproof station beside the oil and gas equipment as its rotors spin up. The drone climbs and flies out over the separator, valves and tank on the well pad. A Texas locator draws an Austin pin and a Permian Basin pin joined by a line as the drone passes over the pad.

The flight software panel lights with a map strip and a status row. An amber alert flag lights on an anomaly marker in the panel. A tag reading the companies say attaches to the alert flag, separating the claim from the record.

An approval letter slides onto the desk and its first lines write in. A date stamp reading September 30th, 2025 lands crooked on the letter. An approved mark lands beside a tag reading periodic methane screening.

The drone hovers above the well pad as its infrared camera pod swings toward the equipment. The drone follows a dashed flight plan to the first numbered point of interest ring above the equipment. An illustrated infrared view of the valve opens as the drone holds at the point of interest.

Survey footage arrives on the review panel showing the illustrated infrared valve. The certified inspector mark lands on the footage and outlines the emission shimmer. A follow-up inspection tag travels from the review panel to the valve on the pad.
The approval letter body scrolls past in rows of text lines. A highlight lands on the letters AI inside the protocol title line. A counter tag reads AI appears once, in a title.

A program tag reading leak reporting by certified third parties settles on the desk. A wall calendar flips to January 22nd, 2027 beside the program tag. A delayed bar slides over the program tag as the calendar page holds.

A calendar page turns to October 7th and a release card lands beside it. A proposal tag reading will propose to rescind attaches to the program tag, unstamped. The proposal tag holds unstamped on the delayed program tag.

The certified inspector mark confirms the emission on the footage and holds. A blank dashed box labelled AI draws beside the footage and stays empty. The drone station stands in the window beside the equipment as the frame holds on the inspector mark and the blank box.

visual_research.decision: No external photograph or footage helps tell this story honestly, so fresh authored illustration performs the sourced method with an Illustration disclosure and no brand marks.

art_direction.palette_reason: Caliche tan carries the Permian pad, galvanized gray steel holds the equipment, warm paper carries the letters and tags, the pale gray of the drone is the one clean value, and a single amber is kept for the alert lamp, stamp and the highlighted AI.
art_direction.shape_language: A compact rounded drone shell against hard rectangular steel vessels, long straight pipe runs and flat paper cards with worn corners. Nothing is symmetric: the post leans, the stamp lands crooked, the highlight overshoots its word.

lighting.motivation: Low warm desert light from the upper left warms the pad, steel and drone shell, cool fill from the right shades the desk scenes, and every grounded thing throws a soft shadow to the right.

hero.silhouette: A compact four-rotor drone with a pale gray shell, a slung infrared camera pod and short legs, sitting in a hooded weatherproof station.
hero.finish: Lit upper-left painted shell with a soft highlight, cool shaded right side, scuffed rotor guards, a dark lens with a small reflection, status lamps and a soft ground shadow on worn steel.

art_direction.focal_hierarchy: The drone or the record first, the inspector mark or the date second, the equipment and the tags third, the pad and the sky last.
art_direction.motion_language: The drone lifts and cruises with continuous acceleration, the route draws at an even speed, cards slide and settle without bounce, stamps and marks land once, and the camera holds while objects perform.

signature_shot.reason: The certified inspector mark lands on the footage and outlines the emission, the whole answer in one movement.

captions.text: Chevron tested autonomous drones from a company located in Austin.
The companies say AI alerts when it detects anomalies to normal operations.
the Environmental Protection Agency approved that company's Air Max drone system for periodic methane screening.
The drone carries an infrared camera
and follows a flight plan to points of interest.
Then a certified inspector reviews the footage to identify any emissions,
The approval letter mentions AI only in the title of a protocol.
EPA also delayed a separate leak reporting program to January 22nd, 2027,
and on October 7th said it will propose to rescind it.
Under this approval, a certified inspector confirms the leak.
The letter doesn't say what the AI adds.
